newsitem.title: USA: NYC Hevesi seen delaying Water Authority debt sale.
newsitem.headline: NYC Hevesi seen delaying Water Authority debt sale.

text.p: The New York City Comptroller, who approves debt sales by the Water Finance Authority, has delayed since February a commercial paper sale of $200 million, a financial source said on Wednesday.

The source, who declined to be named, explained that city Comptroller Alan Hevesi evidently was declining to let the debt sale go through until he wins changes to how about 30 contracts would be handled under a new watershed agreement.
The historic pact, that was signed in January, aims to protect the city's supply of drinking water.
Spokesmen for the Water Finance Authority and the New York City Comptroller, who reviews contracts, declined to comment.
The financial source added that the comptroller's move also put in doubt an approximately $200 million bond sale planned by the water authority for sometime in April: "That's kind of the assumption."

He added that the size of the April bond sale still was being determined as it could be raised if the water authority decided to include a refunding, in addition to using the proceeds to retire commercial paper.
The water authority's last debt sale was in October, 1996, when it sold $360 million of tax-exempt revenue bonds.

Elizabeth St. Clair, the chief of the environmental law division for New York City, said Hevesi's objections to the waterhshed contracts, which add up to about $350 million, focused on technical issues, like procurement. The contracts govern how local governments for a range of tasks, like improving storm sewers and protecting the banks of streams from erroding.
Saying the comptroller had suggested various ways to improve the contracts, St. Clair added the city now was working out the changes it had accepted with local governments.
She was confident that New York City would meet next month's deadline.

"We're supposed to start making payments under the Watershed Agreement by the end of April and I think we'll make that deadline." St. Clair added she had no knowledge of whether any of the Water Finance Authority's debt sales had been delayed.

This is not the first time that the Authority and Hevesi have been on opposite sides of the fence, as the city comptroller has sued the Giuliani Administration to prevent it from selling the water and sewer system.
A decision by the state's highest court is expected this spring.
